title: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Elevated Execution with Prompt
shortTitle: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Elevated Execution wit...
summary: This sub-technique covers adversaries abusing the macOS AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges application programming interface to obtain root without ever stealing a password. The call presents a genuine system credential dialog, so the user supplies an administrator password voluntarily, but the framework never verifies the origin, signature or integrity of the calling program. Attackers pair the call with masquerading, or they backdoor a legitimate installer that already uses the interface, and often point it at world writable helper files that can be swapped after signing. Because each execution is consented to, defenders rarely see it in alerting. The telemetry that reveals it is the authorization subsystem log and unified log entry for the request, combined with the process tree: a freshly written or unsigned parent, or a signed installer whose child is a binary under a user writable path, is the useful discriminator against normal software update behaviour.

beginner.definition: This is a way for a program on a Mac to ask you for your administrator password. If you agree, the program then runs with full system rights, which are called root. The program never has to prove where it came from or that nobody changed it. Attackers use this weakness to reach the highest level of permission on your computer.
beginner.whyItMatters: Full system rights let an attacker install harmful software and change system settings. The attacker can also stay on the machine for a long time. The request looks official, so people type their password without thinking. If your team ignores this, a single normal-looking password prompt can turn into a complete compromise of the Mac.
howItWorks: A program calls the Apple interface that asks for an administrator password to run a task as root.
macOS shows a real system dialog, so the request looks trustworthy to the person at the keyboard.
The program then runs with full system rights, and no check is made on who wrote it.
An attacker may also target a legitimate installer that already uses this weak interface.
If that installer loads files from a folder ordinary users can write to, the attacker swaps in harmful code.
The swapped code runs with the same full system rights, and the signed installer gets the blame.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared flat where a delivery driver rings the bell and asks you to unlock the front door. You check nothing but the uniform, so you press the button. The driver walks in, and now has a key to every room. The building never asked the driver for identification, and it never checked that the parcel was real. That is this weakness. Your one press of the button is treated as proof that the visitor is safe. In truth, it only proves that somebody asked.
takeaways: A password prompt proves that you typed a password, not that the request is safe.
Attackers can gain root by replacing files a trusted installer loads from a writable folder.
Watch for new or unsigned programs that ask for administrator rights on your Macs.

objectives: Explain what the macOS privileged execution interface does and why it does not validate the caller.
Describe how an attacker can gain root rights without stealing any password.
Identify the log and process evidence that separates this abuse from a normal software install.
Explain why a legitimate signed installer can still deliver harmful code as root.
Recognise user-approved elevation as a detection gap and describe one way to reduce it.
